In Maharashtra, Regional Transport Officers have launched a campaign to test taxi and autorickshaw drivers on their practical Marathi through direct oral interactions. Each driver faces a 15-question assessment covering routine commuter queries, with the entire process video-recorded to ensure compliance with revised Motor Vehicle Rules. Those who fail receive a notice and a one-month deadline to improve their language skills.

Failure to meet the requirement results in a three-month badge suspension, and persistent noncompliance can lead to permanent cancellation of driving badges and permits. A Mumbai police officer, clad in a khaki uniform and protective mask, carefully removes a yellow circular sticker from the windshield of a car at a roadside checkpoint. The vehicle’s dashboard holds official papers and a small decorative figurine, while barricades and autorickshaws form a backdrop on the busy city street. The sticker system—red for medical vehicles, green for grocery suppliers, and yellow for civic workers—was introduced to streamline essential travel during COVID-19 lockdowns.

The state police recently reinstated the e-pass system for inter-district and inter-state movement, deeming the dual sticker and e-pass arrangements confusing. Traffic police in Indore intercepted a white Maruti taxi that had been operating without a registration number for two years. The officers, led by Subedar Amit Kumar Yadav and Constable Ashish, pursued the vehicle from IT Park near Tejaji Nagar Square and finally stopped it near the Ralamandal merging point after the driver ignored initial signals.

The private taxi was carrying a family from Uttar Pradesh en route to Maheshwar. After impounding the car and imposing a Rs 6,000 fine on the owner, the officers arranged another taxi for the passengers, ensuring they could continue their journey within 15 minutes.
